--- title: "Training a network" description: "A network keeps improving on its training data long after it stops improving on new data, and two runs from different random starts end in different places. Validation error shows when to stop, and repeated runs show how much the start matters." order: 3 categories: [neural-networks, optimisation, tuning] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## A network's training has to be watched A straight line fitted by gradient descent has one lowest point, and every walk downhill reaches it. A network's loss is different in two ways. With many weights it can keep falling on the training data long after the network has stopped improving on new data, so how long to train is a choice. And the loss has many valleys, so two runs that start from different random weights end in different places. This page shows how validation data decide when to stop, how much the random start changes the result, and how networks are trained on datasets too large to use whole at every step. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.diagram} ![Three things that shape training: validation error says when to stop, the random starting weights decide which valley the walk ends in, and large datasets are walked one small group of rows at a time.](img/training-settings.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. When to stop, early stopping: two curves of error against training steps, training error falling all the way and validation error falling then rising, with a dashed line at its lowest point marked stop here; keep the weights where validation error is lowest; training error keeps falling. Random start, the seed: a wavy loss curve with two valleys and two starting points, start A and start B, each rolling into a different valley; different starting weights end in different valleys; fit several and report the spread. Mini-batches, large datasets: a column of twelve rows in three colours, mixed, and an arrow to the same rows sorted into three groups of four labelled step 1, step 2 and step 3, with a bracket marking one epoch; each step uses a small random group of the rows; one pass through all of them is an epoch."} ::: The number of steps is a hyperparameter, chosen on validation data like the node size on [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). The starting weights are random, so they are not chosen at all; what matters is how much they change the result. Two settings work exactly as in [Gradient descent](../04-how-algorithms-learn/gradient-descent.qmd). The learning rate is tried at values a few times apart: too small crawls, and too large overshoots further on every step until the loss becomes `NaN`, R's "not a number", often with no error or warning. And the inputs are standardised, as [Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd) explains, so that one learning rate suits every weight: put `step_normalize()` in every network's recipe. ## Worked example The network is the one from [Forward propagation and backpropagation](forward-and-backward.qmd): depth, temperature and chlorophyll, standardised, predict abundance on a log scale through one hidden layer of tanh units. This time 200 stations are held back as validation data, so we can watch the network on stations it is not fitted to. `train()` now records the loss on both sets at every step. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() model_data <- survey |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3) |> drop_na() X <- cbind(depth = as.numeric(scale(model_data$depth_m)), temperature = as.numeric(scale(model_data$temperature_c)), chlorophyll = as.numeric(scale(log1p(model_data$chlorophyll_mg_m3)))) y <- log1p(model_data$abundance) set.seed(20) validation <- sample(nrow(X), 200) X_train <- X[-validation, ]; y_train <- y[-validation] X_valid <- X[validation, ]; y_valid <- y[validation] # The same network and passes as on Forward propagation and backpropagation initialise <- function(seed, n_hidden) { set.seed(seed) list(W1 = matrix(rnorm(ncol(X) * n_hidden, 0, 0.5), ncol(X), n_hidden), b1 = rep(0, n_hidden), w2 = rnorm(n_hidden, 0, 0.5), b2 = mean(y_train)) } forward <- function(par, X) { A1 <- tanh(sweep(X %*% par$W1, 2, par$b1, "+")) list(A1 = A1, prediction = as.numeric(A1 %*% par$w2 + par$b2)) } loss <- function(par, X, y) mean((y - forward(par, X)$prediction)^2) backward <- function(par, X, y) { f <- forward(par, X) d_prediction <- -2 * (y - f$prediction) / nrow(X) d_Z1 <- outer(d_prediction, par$w2) * (1 - f$A1^2) list(W1 = t(X) %*% d_Z1, b1 = colSums(d_Z1), w2 = as.numeric(t(f$A1) %*% d_prediction), b2 = sum(d_prediction)) } # Gradient descent on the training stations, scoring both sets after every step train <- function(par, learning_rate, steps) { training <- validation <- numeric(steps) for (step in seq_len(steps)) { gradient <- backward(par, X_train, y_train) for (nm in names(par)) { par[[nm]] <- par[[nm]] - learning_rate * gradient[[nm]] } training[step] <- loss(par, X_train, y_train) validation[step] <- loss(par, X_valid, y_valid) } list(par = par, training = training, validation = validation) } ``` ::: ### Early stopping keeps the weights with the lowest validation error This network has 40 hidden units for 541 training stations, far more than it needs, and trains for 8,000 steps. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} big <- train(initialise(5, 40), learning_rate = 0.05, steps = 8000) best_step <- which.min(big$validation) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(step = seq_along(big$training), Training = big$training, Validation = big$validation) |> pivot_longer(-step, names_to = "set", values_to = "mse") |> ggplot(aes(step, mse, colour = set)) + geom_vline(xintercept = best_step, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#9aa5ad") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + annotate("text", x = best_step, y = 0.95, hjust = 1, size = 3.3, colour = "#77818a", label = paste0("Lowest validation error: step ", fmt_step(best_step), " ")) + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 8000), labels = scales::label_comma()) + labs(x = "Gradient-descent step (log scale)", y = "Mean squared error", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A network with 40 hidden units trained for 8,000 steps. Training error falls throughout. Validation error is lowest at step 1,937 and then rises.](training-a-network_files/figure-html/fig-early-stopping-1.png){#fig-early-stopping fig-alt='Two curves of mean squared error against gradient-descent steps on a log scale. Both start high, training at 1.001 and validation at 1.090, and fall together. The training curve keeps falling, to 0.540 at step 8,000. The validation curve reaches its lowest point, 0.564, at step 1,937, where a dashed vertical line is drawn, then turns upward to 0.589, leaving a widening gap.' width=1500} ::: ::: Training error falls from 1.001 to 0.540 and is still falling at the end. Validation error is lowest at step 1,937, at 0.564, and rises to 0.589 by step 8,000, 4% worse. After step 1,937 the network is learning the training stations' noise. **Early stopping** keeps the weights from the step where validation error was lowest; here it also saves 76% of the steps. Early stopping is a form of regularisation. The weights start small, and a network with small weights is close to linear; training grows them. Stopping early limits how far they grow, which is what the ridge penalty of [Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) does directly. ### The random start changes the score Ten networks with eight hidden units are trained the same way, differing only in the seed that draws their starting weights. Averaging their predictions gives an eleventh model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} seed_runs <- map(1:10, \(seed) train(initialise(seed, 8), learning_rate = 0.2, steps = 3000)) seed_mse <- map_dbl(seed_runs, \(run) last(run$validation)) averaged <- map(seed_runs, \(run) forward(run$par, X_valid)$prediction) |> reduce(`+`) / length(seed_runs) averaged_mse <- mean((y_valid - averaged)^2) tibble(Model = c("Best single network", "Worst single network", "Average of all ten"), `Validation MSE` = round(c(min(seed_mse), max(seed_mse), averaged_mse), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Model | Validation MSE| |:--------------------|--------------:| |Best single network | 0.526| |Worst single network | 0.580| |Average of all ten | 0.548|
::: ::: The ten networks share the data, the settings and the number of steps, yet their validation MSE spans 0.055. That is the seed alone: a network's loss has many valleys, and each start rolls into a different one. Averaging the ten networks' predictions scores 0.548, better than seven of the ten single networks, the same idea as the many trees of [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd). Fit a network several times from different seeds and report the spread. It comes on top of the spread that [Uncertainty and stability](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd) measures by drawing the sites again. On this survey, a difference between two networks smaller than 0.055 could be the seed alone. ## Large datasets are trained in mini-batches Every step on this page uses all 541 training stations to compute the slopes. With hundreds of thousands of rows that is slow, so large networks are trained on **mini-batches**: the rows are shuffled and split into small groups, say of 32, and each step uses one group. This is the stochastic gradient descent that [Gradient descent](../04-how-algorithms-learn/gradient-descent.qmd) named. Each step's slopes are then a noisy estimate, but they cost a fraction of the time, and the noise evens out over many steps. One pass through all the groups is an **epoch**, the usual unit for how long a network trains. ## `mlp()` takes the settings as arguments In tidymodels a network is specified with `mlp()`, for **multilayer perceptron**, the usual name for the networks on these pages. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} network <- mlp(hidden_units = 8, penalty = 0.01, epochs = 500) |> set_engine("nnet") |> set_mode("regression") network_data <- mutate(model_data, log_abundance = log1p(abundance)) network_recipe <- recipe( log_abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3, data = network_data) |> step_log(chlorophyll_mg_m3, offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) set.seed(6) fitted_network <- workflow(network_recipe, network) |> fit(data = network_data[-validation, ]) mlp_predictions <- augment(fitted_network, network_data[validation, ]) mlp_mse <- mean((mlp_predictions$log_abundance - mlp_predictions$.pred)^2) tibble(`Validation MSE` = round(mlp_mse, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Validation MSE| |--------------:| | 0.597|
::: ::: With a small penalty and no early stopping, this network scores 0.597, behind the averaged networks above; the second exercise below tries other penalties. `step_normalize()` standardises the inputs, and `penalty` is the ridge penalty on the weights. `hidden_units` and `penalty` take `tune()` and are chosen by cross-validation, as on [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). `epochs` means something slightly different here: the `nnet` engine does not use gradient descent but BFGS, the search described on [Forward propagation and backpropagation](forward-and-backward.qmd), so it has no learning rate, and `epochs` sets its maximum number of iterations (`maxit`). It still says how long to search. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it Each step of gradient descent moves every weight $w$ against its slope, $w \leftarrow w - \eta \, \partial L / \partial w$, where $\eta$ is the learning rate. With mini-batches, $L$ is the loss on one batch $B$ of rows, $L_B = \frac{1}{|B|} \sum_{i \in B} (y_i - \hat y_i)^2$, so every step sees a different batch. A ridge penalty $\lambda$ adds $\lambda \sum w^2$ to the loss, and the step becomes $w \leftarrow w - \eta \, (\partial L / \partial w + 2 \lambda w)$: every step also pulls each weight a little towards zero. Early stopping limits the same growth by limiting the number of steps. ::: ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A network's training error keeps falling after it stops improving on new data, and its loss has many valleys, so training has to be watched on validation data. - **Early stopping** keeps the weights from the step where validation error is lowest, here step 1,937 of 8,000. It restrains the weights as a penalty does. - Ten runs differing only in their seed varied by 0.055 in validation MSE. Report the spread across seeds, or average several networks. - Set the learning rate and standardise the inputs as for any gradient descent. - Large datasets are trained in **mini-batches**; an **epoch** is one pass through all of them. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Train the 40-unit network with a learning rate of 0.2 instead of 0.05. Is its lowest validation error reached sooner, and is it lower? 2. Change `penalty` in `mlp()` to 0 and then to 1. Which gives the lowest validation MSE, and how does it compare with the averaged networks?
